title: Why stealing an authorization code is not enough
answer: Redeeming the code also needs the verifier, which never passes through the redirect

checks.question: Without PKCE, does redeeming the intercepted code require a secret held by the public client?
checks.answer: No. The attacker still supplies ordinary token-request fields, such as the client ID and matching redirect URI, but these are not client-held secrets. In this exchange the stolen code is enough to impersonate the client.

checks.question: The thief sends the stolen code with a guessed verifier. What does the server compute, and what does it answer?
checks.answer: The base64url SHA-256 of the guess. It differs from the challenge bound to the code, so the server answers invalid_grant.

checks.question: RFC 7636’s example verifier is dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk. Which challenge is bound to the code?
checks.answer: E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM, the base64url encoding of the verifier’s SHA-256.

cases.name: Replay the theft against PKCE: Yes

steps.title: Another app can catch the redirect and redeem its code
steps.line: Predict: the thief has the code and public request fields. What could stop it?
steps.caption: A mobile or desktop app often gets its authorization code back as a redirect to a custom URI scheme. Another app on the device can register the same scheme, and the operating system may hand it the redirect and its code (RFC 7636 §1). This public client has no client secret. The thief knows the ordinary token-request fields, such as the client ID and redirect URI, so presenting the stolen code gets it an access token in this unprotected exchange.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 5 messages. Note: “a token for the wrong app” beside Auth server → Malicious app: Access token; theft: Auth server → Malicious app: Redirect via the shared URI scheme; Malicious app → Auth server: Token request: code; Auth server → Malicious app: Access token.

steps.title: Answer: bind the code to a secret only the real client holds
steps.line: The challenge is the base64url SHA-256 of the verifier.
steps.caption: A fixed secret distributed inside the app can be extracted, so for each sign-in the client instead makes a fresh random code_verifier and keeps it. It sends ahead only the code_challenge, the verifier’s SHA-256 in base64url, a method called S256. Redeeming the code also needs the verifier, which never passes through the redirect. The server can store the challenge now and recognize the right verifier later without learning the secret in advance. The card uses RFC 7636’s example verifier.
steps.picture: Flowchart: 3 nodes, 2 links; 3 labelled values. Travelled: code_verifier → 32-byte digest: SHA-256; 32-byte digest → code_challenge: base64url; marked: code_challenge; code_challenge: E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM.

steps.title: The authorization request carries the challenge and S256
steps.line: It goes through the browser, so treat the challenge as public.
steps.caption: The client sends the challenge and the S256 method in the authorization request, through the user’s browser. The challenge is treated as public; the verifier stays with the client and is not sent. The user then signs in and consents at the auth server.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 1 message. Note: “challenge + S256; verifier not sent” beside Client → Auth server: Authorize request + code_challenge; carries the challenge: Client → Auth server: Authorize request + code_challenge.

steps.title: The redirect carries a short-lived code bound to the challenge
steps.line: Predict: the malicious app catches this code again. What happens when it redeems it?
steps.caption: The server stores the challenge with a short-lived code and redirects the browser back to the client. Because the verifier never travelled, anyone who intercepts this redirect gets only the code, which must still be exchanged for an access token.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 2 messages. Note: “code bound to the challenge” beside Auth server → Client: Redirect with code; carries the code: Auth server → Client: Redirect with code; carries the challenge: Client → Auth server: Authorize request + code_challenge.

steps.title: Answer: invalid_grant. The stolen code fails without the verifier
steps.line: S256 of the guess differs from the challenge bound to the code.
steps.caption: The malicious app gets the redirect and its code as before, but now the token request must carry a verifier too. It can only guess one; S256 of the guess does not match the challenge bound to the code, so the server answers invalid_grant. The displayed prefixes differ already; the server checks the full challenge, not just the prefix.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 5 messages. Attack: Auth server → Malicious app: Redirect via the shared URI scheme; Malicious app → Auth server: Token request: code + a guess; Auth server → Malicious app: invalid_grant; note: “S256(guess) = X4OLkcBH… ≠ E9Melhoa…” beside Auth server → Malicious app: invalid_grant; and 2 more.

steps.title: The token endpoint returns a token only when S256(verifier) matches
steps.line: The real verifier hashes to the bound challenge, so they match.
steps.caption: The real client sends the code with the original verifier. The server computes S256 of the verifier, finds that it matches the challenge stored with the code, and returns an access token once its usual code and client checks also pass.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 7 messages. Accepted: Client → Auth server: Token request: code + code_verifier; Auth server → Client: Access token; note: “S256(verifier) = E9Melhoa… = bound challenge” beside Auth server → Client: Access token; carries the challenge: Client → Auth server: Authorize request + code_challenge; and 4 more.

steps.title: The verifier never travels where the code does
steps.line: Challenge and code pass the browser; the verifier goes by TLS.
steps.caption: The challenge and the code pass through the browser and the operating system, where another app can read them. The verifier, made from 32 random bytes, goes only in the client’s own TLS request to the token endpoint. Finding a verifier that matches its S256 challenge is computationally infeasible, so catching the redirect does not give the thief a practical way to redeem the code. This protection depends on keeping the verifier secret.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 7 messages. Note: “The verifier, 32 random bytes, went only by TLS” beside Auth server → Client: Access token; readable on the device: Client → Auth server: Authorize request + code_challenge; Auth server → Client: Redirect with code; Auth server → Malicious app: Redirect via the shared URI scheme; and 1 more.
